newsitem.title: UK: Adams says London must act to save N.Irish peace.
newsitem.headline: Adams says London must act to save N.Irish peace.

text.p: Roman Catholic leaders piled pressure on IRA guerrillas on Tuesday to call a truce, but Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said it was up to Britain to breathe life into the faltering Northern Ireland peace process.

A leading Protestant politician linked to pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas said they would "obviously...re-assess the situation" following Monday's announcement by jailed Loyalists they had lost faith in the province's peace process.

The Loyalist prisoners' decision, following a string of IRA bomb attacks in mainland Britain and a foiled bomb attack by republican dissidents in Belfast, heightened fears that pro-British gunmen might resume hostilities against Catholics.

John White, leader of the Ulster Democratic Party, said sectarian bloodshed could return to Northern Ireland if the IRA launched more attacks aimed at ending rule from London, but he believed the truce would hold "at this moment".
"If there is any reaction from Sinn Fein/IRA, then it makes it much more difficult and there is every likelihood that there could be a return to full-scale conflict," said White.
Loyalists answered an IRA truce in September 1994 with their own ceasefire in October. The IRA ended their truce with bombs in London in February but the Loyalists' ceasefire still holds.

Cardinal Cahal Daly, retiring as spiritual head of the sland's five million Roman Catholics, agreed violence by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) was the chief obstacle to its Sinn Fein political arm getting a place at peace talks.
"No single thing would do more at this time to restore hope and lessen division in our society than a reinstatement of the IRA ceasefire," Daly told reporters in Armagh, west of Belfast.

Leading Catholic politician Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, said the Loyalists' statement had created a "serious situation, a potential threat to the peace process." He also called for an IRA ceasefire.
"I believe they (the IRA) have it in their power to ensure that the apprehension in the community recedes and that the peace process can be built on," Mallon told reporters in Belfast.
But Adams, leader of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, said Britain should learn from peace efforts in the Middle East and allow his party into the talks.
Britain and Ireland launched their joint peace plan in late 1993, which led to the twin ceasefires. But multi-party talks have become bogged down in administrative details.

"The British government has yet to create the climate or indeed the practicalities for real talks," Adams said. "There were disastrous events in the Middle East... Today in Washington the (rival) leaders are meeting."

"Compare that to what is happening here, when people are being cut-out, marginalised, excluded. John Major should take example." U.S. President Bill Clinton was meeting Israeli Prime MInister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat separately at the White House on Tuesday.

Around 1,000 Loyalist and IRA prisoners in Belfast are frustrated Britain did not respond to the 1994 ceasefires by announcing an amnesty. Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said he could understand the frustration felt by prisoners but violence was not the answer.
"I certainly would hope that it is not a return to violence because once violence resumes on their side then I think the scenario becomes very bleak on all sides," he told Irish radio.

IRA bombs in Britain, and discoveries such as last week's haul of 10 tonnes of explosives in London, have fed fears that despite talk of peace the IRA remains as determined as ever to use force to end British rule.
